mappings.note: Two equal coils used singly, in series and in parallel (LO-2), with I = V/R each time (LO-1). No heat output is asked for, so despite the oven context C 2.5-LO-2 is not graded. Flag: the stem says a 200 V line but the stored answer works throughout at 220 V.

Brightness is power per bulb, so C 2.5-LO-1 leads; the comparison and the one-bulb-fuses question both turn on how series and parallel behave (LO-2). Kept off C 2.5-LO-2 because nothing about the filament's heating mechanism is graded.

Part (i) demands a labelled circuit diagram (LO-5) and the V-to-I relation it establishes (LO-1); part (ii) is a separate geometry problem, halved length and doubled area (LO-3). The two halves share no data.

Four sub-parts, three slots: mixed-combination equivalent resistance (LO-2), Joule's law and the fuse rating (C 2.5-LO-2), and I = P/V for the 1 kW iron (C 2.5-LO-1). Part (d), why a bulb and a heater cannot share a series circuit, also belongs to LO-2 and so costs no extra code.

Derives the three-resistor parallel rule from I = I1 + I2 + I3 with Ohm's law on each branch, then finds the minimum arrangement of four equal resistors. A derive-plus-design item, so LO-1 is cited as the working engine rather than as a separate answer.

Defines power, then computes P = VI and energy in kWh (C 2.5-LO-1); the middle sub-part R = V/I is Ohm's law on measured values (C 2.4-LO-1). Note part (a)'s stored answer defines power mechanically as 'rate of doing work' rather than electrically.
R = V^2/P from the rating, then kWh for three bulbs over a month, then the bill. All three sub-parts sit inside LO-1, so a single code is the honest answer rather than a manufactured spread.
Three distinct demands: the meaning of one ohm (C 2.4-LO-1), the definition of power and P = V^2/R (C 2.5-LO-1), and how many equal resistors in parallel give a target line current (C 2.4-LO-2).

State the law, draw the V-I graph, substitute one pair of values. A near-verbatim duplicate of item 255 in part 10 and mapped identically; C 8.1 carries the graphical half because LO-5 covers only circuit diagrams and meters.

Cutting into four parts is LO-3 (and the invariance of rho is the graded trap), recombining them in series and parallel is LO-2, and the final part asks which combination consumes more power at fixed voltage (C 2.5-LO-1). Three separately marked steps.
Disadvantages of series household wiring and an effective-resistance reduction, both LO-2; LO-5 because the stem gives no resistor values and the network exists only in the figure.
Third re-set of the three-parallel-resistors question, here 10/20/30 ohm on 12 V. Same three graded steps as items 200, 207 and 252; I record the shared codes rather than inventing a difference.
Ammeter current is asked for explicitly (LO-5), reached through a series-plus-parallel reduction (LO-2) and V = IR for the two PDs (LO-1). The stem carries no values at all.

Part (a) is an experimental design - move the ammeter around a series loop and compare readings - which is LO-5's meter clause used as evidence; part (b) is the series sum (LO-2) and V = IR across one resistor (LO-1).

Asks for a circuit diagram including ammeter, voltmeter and key (LO-5), the derivation of the parallel expression (LO-2) with Ohm's law per branch (LO-1), and then a network evaluation. The drawing requirement is explicit, so LO-5 leads.

Proof of the reciprocal rule (LO-2) via branch Ohm's law (LO-1), with a supporting circuit diagram (LO-5). Differs from the previous item only in that the numerical half is a plain two-resistor current, so the proof carries the weight and LO-2 leads.
Series total (LO-2), circuit current and the two PDs by V = IR (LO-1), then the lamp's power (C 2.5-LO-1). The power sub-part is what separates this from the otherwise identical series-circuit items.
Design task: arrange three equal resistors to hit two target values. Pure LO-2 worked backwards, with no supply, current or power anywhere in the item.

Part (a) states Joule's law (LO-2) and part (b) computes the line current for two rated lamps in parallel (C 2.5-LO-1 for the ratings, C 2.4-LO-2 for the parallel combination). Note the two halves are unrelated: Joule's law is never used in the calculation.
Eight data pairs to be plotted, with R taken from the slope. C 8.1 for building and reading the graphical model; LO-1 for the resistance it yields. Same family as the other plot-and-find-R items.

Defines current, gives I = Q/t, then computes charge for 0.75 A over 15 minutes. Both halves are the definition of current, which no outcome covers; the competency is the only legal home. Content gap.
Defines power, defines the watt, and derives P = VI from W/t. A statement-and-derivation item rather than a substitution one, but entirely within LO-1.
Multi-appliance monthly bill in units at a given rate - the fullest kWh-and-billing item in the chapter, and still a single outcome because nothing but power and time is used.

Plot, compute R as a mean of three slopes, and say what the graph represents. The averaging of slopes is data-handling (C 8.1), the resistance itself is LO-1. Note the tabulated pair (2.0 A, 6.2 V) is slightly off the line, which is what forces the mean.

States Ohm's law and substitutes 2 V / 1 A (LO-1), and requires the verification circuit with ammeter and voltmeter (LO-5). The graph sub-part would want C 8.1 as well, but LO-5 is kept because the drawn circuit is the explicitly marked representation.
